content.thinking:
Since I can't run a typecheck tool here, I'll be careful with the API and keep things conservative. I'm sketching the capybara design: roughly 1.1m long and 0.55m tall, with a barrel-shaped body, blunt boxy snout, small ears, tiny eyes, and a whimsical rounded look.

Now I'm planning a small bird perched on its head for a playful touch, giving it its own rig with body, head, wings, tail, and legs. I'm also laying out the skeleton coordinates—hips as root, a spine chain running forward to the chest, then neck, head, and jaw joints, plus a tail chain—figuring out joint positions so the proportions read correctly with the floor at y=0.

I'm sketching how the body loft will follow the spine chain, with the rump extending slightly behind the hips joint, trying to reason through how the loft stations and bone list should connect so the rear end caps off smoothly.

I'm defining the loft stations along the spine with centers, widths, and heights that taper from the rump through the barrel to the chest, then figuring where the legs attach beneath the body based on the lowest point of the torso.

For color, I'm picking a warm golden-brown fur palette with a lighter belly and darker accents, planning a custom paint function that blends these tones by surface normal and adds noise grain for a natural coat texture.

Still writing fur color logic...

Now I'm thinking about the head shape -- capybara heads are large and blocky with a long snout, attached via a short neck joint.

I'll shape the skull as a loft from back to nose, narrowing and flattening slightly toward the muzzle with rounded caps at each end, all rigged to the single head joint for now, with the lower jaw split off as a separate part later.

For facial features, I'm considering a dark flattened sphere for the nose pad with nostril marks, and for the eyes I'm leaning toward simple textured spheres placed high and to the sides of the head rather than fiddly decals on the loft surface, aiming for a slightly oversized, sleepy-lidded, whimsical look.

I'll make the eye symmetric to avoid mirroring issues, with a droopy fur-colored lid covering the top third for a serene contented look, using a dark oval with highlights underneath. For ears, I'll add small rounded shapes near the top-back of the head with darker pink inner spheres, positioning the bird to sit centered between them atop the head.

Placing the bird at the head's top, I'm planning it as a small whimsical sky-blue bird with a cream belly, orange beak, and tiny crest tuft, rigged with its own joint hierarchy (body, head, upper/lower beak, wing chains, tail, and legs) all parented to the head joint.

That lines up fine, feet sunk slightly into the fur. For whimsy, I'm considering small extra touches like a tiny flower tucked behind the capybara's ear, while keeping the bird-on-head as the main playful detail without cluttering the scene further.

Now I'm scattering small fur tuft cards across the capybara's body for texture, using a couple of tinted greyscale or pre-colored brown tuft textures mixed together rather than relying on paint parameters per card.

For whiskers, I'm adding a few thin dark sweeps on each side of the muzzle. For the legs, I'm setting up IK chains for the short, thick limbs — front legs with four toes, hind legs with three webbed toes — defining shoulder-to-foot targets and segment lengths so the knees bend slightly backward for a natural stance.

I'm working out the hind leg chain with its root, mid, and foot target points, then figuring out the naming convention: three points with three names (shoulder, elbow, hand/wrist) represent a chain ending at the tip joint, assigning roles like "leg" or "arm" to each limb accordingly.

Now I'm thinking through sweeping the legs as tapered capsule shapes with a thinning radius function, making sure rounded caps hide the junction where the leg meets the body. For feet, I'm planning flattened sphere shapes attached at the tip joint, with small toe capsules added near the foot's forward tip.

Working through the toe and foot geometry, checking that each sphere and capsule aligns so the bottom surfaces stay flush with the ground rather than sinking below or floating above it.

Then I'm adjusting the leg IK lengths so the front and hind legs reach their foot targets with a slight knee bend rather than being perfectly straight, which should keep the chunky leg proportions looking natural.

For the hind legs with three segments, I need four joint names—hip, knee, hock, and a tip name for the foot. I'm also checking that leg attachment points at the shoulder stay inside the body silhouette so the legs don't poke outside the torso width.

Since capybaras lack a visible tail, I'm adding just a tiny nub chain with one or two joints and a small sweep radius for the rump bump. Now I'm working out the neck chain path, running from the chest area up toward the head, and figuring out how it should parent off the last joint of the spine chain.

Defining head and jaw joints...

Checking the silhouette continuity, the head blends smoothly into the body, matching how real capybaras merge head and torso. I'm reconsidering proportions since my head-to-body ratio runs long compared to real capybara dimensions, but decide the oversized head suits the whimsical style, so I'm adjusting head station measurements to blend more gradually into the body.

I'll keep the overall size as is, slightly chubby and whimsical. For the body shape I'll use 10-sided sections for a blocky puppet look, and I'll add a dark nose bulb as a flattened sphere positioned near the top-front of the muzzle.

Now I'm working out the mouth details: a small lower jaw box beneath the muzzle in a cream tone, plus a whimsical smile line draped along the sides of the snout using curved path geometry.

I realize the full cranium loft would swallow the jaw if left as-is, so I need to shrink the head loft's height so the mouth line sits properly at the boundary, with a separate chin piece underneath.

I'll simplify by skipping the surface drape for the smile line and trust the catmull path approach, weighted to the jaw bone. For cheeks, I'll add blush using a hard-edged pink oval decal with a few tiny lines rather than a soft gradient. Now I'm working out eye placement relative to the skull center.

Writing eye texture SVG...

I should clip the lid to the eye circle instead, using a clipPath so the fur rectangle only shows within the circular region, keeping edges transparent outside it. Then I'll place soft highlights in the lower visible portion of the eye for a sleepy half-lid look, skipping lashes or brows for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the capybara ears: small, rounded, with dark rims, positioned at the top-back sides of the head using flattened spheres for the outer ear and smaller pink flattened spheres for the inner ear, oriented outward and upward with appropriate scale and rotation.

Next I'm placing a small whimsical bird perched between the ears on top of the head, sized to fit the gap, and starting to design its round chick-like bluebird shape.

Now I'm working out the bird's body proportions: a fluffy oval body sitting just above the head's surface with tiny legs tucked underneath, a raised rounded head toward the front, and a small orange beak protruding forward.

I'm adding tiny bead eyes with white highlights and cheek blush, then planning the wings as rigged joint chains with flattened feather-like sweeps curving back along the body sides.

Now I'm planning the tail as a two-joint chain sweeping upward and back from the rump, flattened horizontally with a wide, thin cross-section and small forked tip feathers. I'm also adding a small curling crest tuft of three dark-blue spikes on top of the head.

For the legs, I'm building two thin orange rod chains from hip to foot, naming the joints so they can attach small toe capsules extending forward from each foot.

For coloring, I'm going with an eastern bluebird palette: blue back, orange chest fading to cream belly, using a position-based paint function to blend the gradient across the body sphere.

I'm thinking about adding a lighter throat tone to the head, then considering small whimsical touches for the bird—like a slightly open beak for singing—and for the capybara, extras like a tucked flower, rosy cheeks, freckles, and fur-tuft eyebrows to keep things playful without overcomplicating the design.

Now I'm placing small cream-yellow incisor shapes under the upper lip for that signature capybara buck-tooth smile, and tallying up the texture list I'll need—eye, fur tuft highlights and shadows, blush, and a flower petal decal—to make sure there's enough visual variety.

I'm also sketching in dot-pattern decals on the muzzle sides to suggest whisker clusters, figuring out their angular placement relative to the head's center so they land naturally on the snout surface.

Rather than estimating hit points by angle, I'll switch to using nearest-surface-point lookups for placing both the muzzle dots and the eyes, since that gives a predictable position and normal direction to project the decal along. I'm working through the approximate coordinates for the eye position near the top side of the head, checking that the head's width at that depth keeps the eye placement within the surface bounds.

For the eyes, I'll override the automatic normal direction with an explicit forward-tilted direction so they read as visible from the front rather than foreshortened sideways, keeping the up vector default and using a moderate segment count for the decal. I'll apply the same nearest-point approach for a cheek blush decal, then move on to building a daisy flower behind the ear using a ring of petals anchored at the ear base.

For the petals themselves, I'm using scaled sphere geometry stretched along one axis so each petal radiates outward in the flower's plane, with the ring arrangement orienting each petal to face outward from the center based on the flower's facing direction.

Now I'm placing a yellow sphere at the flower center and positioning the whole flower near the left ear, angled with a diagonal facing direction. I need to figure out which bone/joint this should attach to, since without an explicit bone it should default to the nearest joint—likely something around the head or jaw area given its position.

Rather than relying on ambiguous nearest-joint logic, I decide to explicitly pass the bone option as "head" in the stick call to avoid any guessing, even though the convention is usually to omit bone unless rigidity is needed. For the petals, I'll use a ring loop with angle steps, keeping in mind angle 0 points toward world up. No hair tufts needed between the ears since this capybara doesn't have them. For the fur, I'm setting up a scatter of around 260 cards across the body surface, filtered by normal direction and minimum spacing, with a small card size.

I'm working out how the fur card orientation interacts with lean angle and flow direction -- with a 70-degree lean, the cards lie mostly flat along the surface so they read as face-on blades from outside rather than edge-on slivers, which is the look I want. I'm also planning smaller secondary fur patches for cheek ruffs and chin, skipping legs and elbows for now to keep things simple. For whiskers, I'm setting up three bezier sweeps per side starting near the muzzle and curving downward and forward toward the tips.

Now I'm turning to toes and claws -- front feet get four toes, hind feet three, built as capsule shapes fanning forward from the foot center with blunt nail tips. I'm deciding on a skin-brown toe color with a darker nail tip, possibly using a small dark sphere or cone for the claw itself to keep it blunt and hoof-like rather than sharp.

I'm thinking through leg sweep radii next: shoulders taper from thicker at top to narrower near the foot, hind thighs are even bulkier before tapering, and I'm leaning on the coat's existing paint gradient to darken the lower leg rather than adding separate shading geometry. I'm considering whether to add a haunch bulge sphere at the hip but may skip it since the body shape already reads wide enough.

Now I'm tallying up the total part count across body, head, ears, eyes, whiskers, legs, feet, toes, thighs, tail, and decorative elements like flowers and cards -- landing around 100-130, which is below my target range of 180-340, so I need to add more detail like neck ruff, eyebrow tufts, nostril marks, and toenail accents to bulk it out.

I'm deciding against extra accessories like a scarf or collar since the pitch is simple -- capybara with bird, maybe one small flower is enough. Instead I'll flesh out toenails and bird details like feather tips and eye rings, plus add cheek puff spheres near the capybara's muzzle for a chunkier, blockier look.

I'm also shading the coat: darkening along the spine where the normal faces upward, and adding a darker muzzle mask toward the front of the face using smooth blending zones.

For the rest of the body, I'm lightening the belly where the normal points downward, darkening the feet near the ground, and applying a subtle noise streak for texture variation, with the ear using its own separate coloring. The paint resolution depends on model-space positions at the build pose.

For the bird, I'm adding eye detail with a small black sphere and a tiny white highlight offset for shine, plus cone shapes for the beak.

Now I'm sketching out the beak geometry as spike sweeps — an upper beak attached to the head bone pointing forward and slightly down, and a shorter, thinner lower beak attached to the jaw joint below it. Then I'm starting on the bird's skeleton, defining the body joint parented to the head with a forward-angled direction, and beginning the head joint next.

Continuing the skeleton, I'm placing the head and jaw joints with specific positions and directions, then considering a small downward pose rotation on the jaw to suggest a slightly open beak -- though I catch myself drifting into capybara jaw details that don't belong here and refocus on keeping the bird's beak closed or barely open.

Now I'm building the bird's body parts: a low-poly sphere scaled down for the torso, keeping smooth shading rather than faceted since a whimsical rounded look suits the body better. I'm positioning a smaller scaled sphere for the head near the top of the body.

Adding eye spheres and wing bone chains...

Setting up the tail chain now, with joint positions tapering backward from the body and a sweep radius that narrows toward the tip, using rounded end caps and a thin vertical profile.

Then I'm defining the leg chain for the bird with hip and foot joint positions, making sure the IDs don't collide with the tail naming, and adding toe capsules extending forward and one backward from each foot for a realistic bird stance.

I'm also checking the loft geometry's height at the bird's z position, interpolating between the nearby station widths/heights to confirm the head top sits around y≈0.68 there, which tells me where to actually place the bird so it rests correctly on the surface.

Rather than hardcoding that estimate, I decide to use a ray cast straight down onto the head loft surface at the bird's x/z position to get the exact top height, which is cleaner than guessing. I'm also checking that the bird's position doesn't cause its tail to overlap with the ears geometrically, since both occupy similar z-ranges near the front of the head.

I should also add neck ruff cards and rump fur cards for the capybara, letting the scatter fur cover the hind end. For the tail, I'll just include a tiny stub piece rather than a full chain since capybaras barely have tails.

Looking at the body rig, the cards should take the loft's bone weights, and I can feed the IK limb's returned point array directly into the chain function since it accepts arrays of points as a path input -- the smooth skin will round out any sharp corners from the polyline. I'll import the limb function to set up root and target positions for the legs.

Working out the geometry, I'm computing distances between root and target positions for front and hind legs to make sure they fit within the total bone length, and choosing bend directions so joints flex naturally. I'm naming the joints shoulder, elbow, hand for front legs and hip, knee, hock, foot for hind legs, with left/right suffixes based on side.

For parenting, I'm placing front legs under the third spine joint near the chest, and hind legs under the hips, with a three-joint spine chain interpolated along a catmull curve from hips to chest. The neck chain then starts where the spine chain ends, and the overall body skeleton sweeps from hips through spine to neck.

I'm reconsidering where the hips joint should actually sit relative to the rear of the spine curve -- maybe placing hips further back near the tail base so the thighs attach closer to their natural position, rather than at the exact spine origin.

Adding a tail/rump chain running backward from the hips with two segments to cover the rear body, matching the same parenting pattern used for the spine and neck chains. The tail path extends slightly beyond the main body loft, which should be fine for coverage.

Now I'm setting up helper constants for symmetry before writing the actual bone creation code.

Defining the fur color palette with warm golden tones for highlights, shadows, belly, and muzzle, aiming for a whimsical but slightly saturated capybara look. I'm sketching out the SVG tuft textures for fur detail, starting with a blade-shaped path using darker edge coloring.

Still writing SVG blade shapes...

Still planning texture details... for the muzzle dots and eye, then considering whether flowers need actual geometry versus a flat daisy/leaf texture card instead.

Now I'm working out two leaves behind each flower using an extruded outline for a simple leaf shape, positioning them at the flower base so they point outward roughly flat in the tangent plane.

Actually, I can place the flower by finding the nearest point on the head surface, using the hit normal for orientation, then arranging petals in a ring around that point, with each petal a small flattened sphere oriented to face radially outward.

Translating the geometry so its base sits at zero, then placing the flower center as a small yellow sphere offset slightly above its origin. For the smile, I'm working through where the mouth line should sit relative to the muzzle loft sections—checking the head's front cap position and jaw height to figure out a believable mouth placement on the capybara's face.

Now I'm positioning the lower jaw as a small box beneath the mouth line, sizing it narrower than the muzzle loft so it tucks under without poking through the sides of the head shape.

For the smile line, I'm plotting a curved path of points that hug the surface from the mouth corner up through the cheek to a slight upturn near the eye, then sweeping a thin dark tube along it to render the crease.

Now I'm working out the teeth geometry—placing two small cream boxes at the mouth's center front, figuring out where the dome-shaped head surface intersects that y-level so the teeth sit flush against the face.

Actually, sticking a box along the normal would make it poke forward-down, not hang down like real teeth. I should instead place each tooth explicitly below the lip using a ray cast straight down from the face to find the surface z-position, then offset slightly inward for visibility.

For the nose, I'll cast a ray down to find the front face z at the right height, then place a slightly flattened dark sphere protruding just beyond that surface, plus tiny darker ellipsoid nostrils and a small highlight dot for shine. I'm checking that the protrusion amount looks natural rather than piercing through the head.

I'll scatter cheek ruff tufts across the head using a surface loft with a minimum distance filter, excluding points near the muzzle front, and keep eyebrows simple with just the sleepy lid line doing the expressive work. I'm also considering subtle freckle-like patches via noise in the coat material before starting the final implementation code.

Writing the component imports and setup...

Still writing shading logic...

I'm adding a cool tint toward the belly's underside to complete the countershading gradient, then setting up the bird's color palette with blue back tones and warm cream chest/belly colors for its own countershaded body.

Working out countershading for the head similarly, then starting to build out the capybara skeleton structure with joint hierarchy...

Adding tail and spine chains...

Checking that parent references accept a Chain's last joint, confirming that pattern works. Now I'm building the body loft with cross-sections defining width and height along the spine...

Checking the body's rounded cap doesn't bulge past the head width — the front end radius is wider than the head's starting width, which could create a visible bulge around the neck junction.

Now I'm lofting the skull shape with tapering stations from the base near the neck out to the snout tip at .70, using a 10-sided profile. The real capybara snout is blocky, so I'm considering whether to keep smooth circular sides or switch to a faceted n-gon to preserve that chunky silhouette.

I'm placing eye decals using nearest-surface lookups on the head loft, positioning them symmetrically with explicit direction and size parameters, and double-checking whether an explicit dir overrides the surface normal.

Now I'm checking the ear placement coordinates against the skull dimensions at that z-depth to make sure they land correctly on the surface.

Writing ear geometry code...

Still working out whisker geometry...

I'll skip the forehead fur tuft since the bird sits there anyway. Now scattering fur cards across the body surface with randomized placement, size, lean, and spin parameters.

I'm checking that the body-side filter excludes tufts near the head, and planning a head ruff with similar filtering but also excluding the eye decal areas so tufts don't cover the eyes.

I'll add a separate scatter for jaw-side tufts with their own size and flow direction, then move on to building the leg/foot function with toe count and spread parameters, importing the Joint type from the skeleton module.

Writing foot pad geometry...

Still writing leg loop...

Now setting up the hind leg chain with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints, tapering the sweep radius down the leg, and adding a thigh bulge sphere near the hip joint for muscle definition.

Still placing bird joints...

Still shaping the beak geometry...

Now I'm placing the eyes: small ink-colored spheres with a tiny highlight offset toward the front-top for sparkle, sized a bit larger for charm, plus optional blush discs on the cheeks for a friendly touch.

For the crest, I'm adding three curved bezier sweeps rising from the top of the head, tapering to a point and sweeping back and upward, forming the bird's signature plume.

Now I'm filling in wings, tail, and legs per the existing plan, and considering whether to skip small fluff tufts as unnecessary detail. For the flower placement, I'm positioning it near the left ear so it sits close to the bird without overlapping its wing or legs, checking the x and z coordinates to keep the petals clear of the bird's body.

Repositioning the flower to the side of the head, behind the ear and below it, facing outward so it reads well from a side view, and confirming the skull width still fits. Now I'm working out the leaf geometry, orienting them vertically along the flower's plane so they extrude flat against the side of the head.

Checking the perpendicularity of the two leaf axis vectors confirms they're orthogonal, so leaf2 points backward-up symmetrically to leaf1's backward-down orientation, with the cross product giving the thickness direction along X for proper facing.

Now I'm planning the petal ring arrangement around the hit point and sketching the center sphere geometry, scaling it along y and offsetting slightly for embedding depth.

Positioning the ring and sphere along the normal offset so petals sit just above the surface without clipping. Then placing the muzzle dot decals and blush markings using nearest-point coordinates with appropriate size and direction.

I'm also double-checking some API details—confirming that chain contact options, part scale arrays, joint group settings, and loft sides parameters all exist as expected before relying on them.

Now I'm working out the leg rod sweep with a thin radius, then setting up the wing chain naming and joint points, and adding feather spike tips at the last wing joint with coordinates tied to the base wing position.

Next I'm figuring out the tail root and tip points with an upward angle, checking the body's z extents, and verifying the overall bird height adds up correctly against the head and crest positions.

Now I'm double-checking ear placement relative to body width, confirming the spine joint coloring, and deciding to skip leg tufts for simplicity. I'm about to write the eye SVG elements and whisker dots, then move on to writing the full file, while sorting out how to color the chin fur and jaw area with a slightly lighter tone than the main coat.

I'm positioning the jaw frustum box so it tucks slightly behind the muzzle for a cute chin effect, adjusting its front edge to meet the head's curved underside without clipping, and skipping teeth or tongue details for now.

For the mouth, I'm building smile curves on each side using catmull-rom points draped onto the head's surface, then sweeping thin tubes along them with rounded cross-sections so the smile lines hug the face naturally from both sides.

Now I'm adding a philtrum groove between the nose and mouth, then computing the nose position by raycasting against the head surface to place the nose sphere and nostrils symmetrically around the resulting front-facing z-coordinate.

Writing eye SVG markup...

Adjusting lid curve for a sleepy look...

Now I need to move on to the full module structure, covering beak colors and foot/toe joint geometry — figuring out span counts from joint names and placing toe positions relative to foot height and depth.

Checking the leg chain lengths against body bottom and foot height to make sure proportions line up, then mentally verifying types compile correctly across the surface sweep, eye point arrays, and limb bend parameters before finalizing the code.
